scenarios.title: Cardiology Referral for Second Opinion

narrative.situation:
Dr. Sarah Chen is a general cardiologist at Memorial Hospital in Hartford, Connecticut. One of her patients, James Walker, a 62-year-old retired postal worker, came in last Tuesday complaining of shortness of breath and occasional chest pain during light exercise. After performing an echocardiogram and a cardiac MRI, Dr. Chen identified what appears to be moderate-to-severe aortic valve regurgitation with early signs of left ventricular dilation.

Given the complexity of the case and the possibility that James may need a valve replacement, Dr. Chen wants to send his imaging results, echocardiogram report, and relevant medical history to Dr. Priya Patel, a cardiac surgeon at University Medical Center across town, for a second opinion. James verbally agreed to the referral during his last appointment, though no formal written authorization was signed.

The hospital's medical records department is preparing to transmit the records electronically through their secure health information exchange system. The records include James's cardiac MRI images, echocardiogram measurements, medication list (including warfarin and metoprolol), and a summary note from Dr. Chen describing her clinical findings and concerns.
narrative.question: Is Memorial Hospital permitted to send James Walker's cardiac imaging results and medical history to Dr. Priya Patel at University Medical Center for a second opinion on potential valve replacement surgery?

scenarios.title: Insurance Company Requesting Surgical Records

narrative.situation:
Robert Kim, a 55-year-old software engineer, underwent a total knee replacement at St. Luke's Medical Center in Houston three months ago. The surgery was performed by Dr. Jennifer Walsh, an orthopedic surgeon, after conservative treatments failed to manage Robert's severe osteoarthritis.

BlueCross BlueShield of Texas, Robert's health insurer, has sent a formal request to St. Luke's medical records department for the complete surgical records associated with Robert's knee replacement. The insurer needs the operative report, anesthesia records, pre-operative assessments, post-operative notes, and physical therapy referrals to process Robert's claim, which totals approximately $47,000. Robert's employer-sponsored plan requires documentation of medical necessity for joint replacement procedures exceeding $30,000.

St. Luke's billing department has confirmed that Robert's policy is active and that the claim is pending. The medical records coordinator, Angela Torres, is preparing the records package. She wants to make sure the hospital can legally send these records to the insurer without needing Robert to sign a specific authorization form for this disclosure. Angela cross-checks the insurer's request against Robert's full chart and includes only the specific items BlueCross BlueShield asked for -- the operative report, anesthesia records, pre-operative assessments, post-operative notes, and physical therapy referrals -- leaving out unrelated portions of his medical history, such as an unrelated dermatology visit from earlier in the year.
narrative.question: Can St. Luke's Hospital send Robert Kim's complete knee replacement surgical records to BlueCross BlueShield to process his insurance claim without a separate written authorization from Robert?

scenarios.title: Mother Asking About Child's ER Visit

narrative.situation:
Maria Rodriguez brought her six-year-old daughter, Sofia, to the emergency department at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia after Sofia fell off the monkey bars during recess at Elm Street Elementary School. The school nurse called Maria at work, and she rushed to the hospital where an ambulance had already transported Sofia.

Upon arrival, Maria found Sofia in a treatment room with a temporary splint on her left arm. The ER attending physician, Dr. Kevin Park, had already ordered X-rays and was waiting for the radiologist's read. Sofia was tearful but stable, with no signs of head injury or loss of consciousness.

Maria is Sofia's biological mother and sole legal custodian — Sofia's parents divorced two years ago, and Maria has full custody per the family court order. Maria wants to know exactly what the X-rays showed, what the treatment plan is, whether Sofia will need surgery, and how long recovery might take. She's also asking for copies of all records to share with Sofia's pediatrician, Dr. Hernandez, at her next follow-up visit.

Dr. Park is preparing to discuss the imaging findings with Maria. The X-rays show a displaced fracture of the distal radius that will likely require closed reduction under sedation.
narrative.question: Can Dr. Park share Sofia's X-ray results, diagnosis, and treatment plan with Maria, Sofia's mother and legal custodian?

scenarios.title: Pastor Checking on Hospitalized Parishioner

The hospital's compliance officer, Dr. Richard Yang, has been called to review the request and determine whether disclosure is appropriate under HIPAA.

scenarios.title: County Health Department Requesting TB Patient Data

narrative.situation:
The Maricopa County Department of Public Health in Arizona has identified a cluster of tuberculosis cases traced to a shared workplace — a large distribution warehouse employing over 200 workers. Eight confirmed cases have been reported in the past six weeks, suggesting active transmission within the facility.

Dr. Elena Vasquez, the county epidemiologist, has sent an official request to Valley Medical Center, where most of the affected workers received care, requesting the names, contact information, and TB test results of all patients who tested positive for TB at the facility in the past 90 days. This information is needed to conduct contact tracing, identify additional exposed individuals, and implement infection control measures at the warehouse.

The health department cites Arizona Revised Statutes §36-714, which requires health care providers to report cases of tuberculosis to the local health department, and the federal Public Health Service Act, which authorizes health departments to collect disease surveillance data. Dr. Vasquez has provided the statutory references in her request letter.

Valley Medical Center's infection control nurse, Patricia Huang, has compiled the requested information and is seeking approval from the hospital's compliance office before releasing it.
narrative.question: May Valley Medical Center disclose the names, contact information, and TB test results of positive patients to the Maricopa County Department of Public Health for outbreak investigation and contact tracing?

scenarios.title: University Researcher Requesting De-Identified Records

narrative.situation:
Professor Lisa Park from the School of Public Health at State University is conducting a five-year longitudinal study on opioid prescribing patterns and their correlation with emergency department visits across rural communities. The study has been funded by the National Institutes of Health and has received IRB approval from the university.

Professor Park has approached Regional Medical Center, a 200-bed community hospital serving three rural counties, about obtaining patient data for her research. After discussions with the hospital's research coordinator, they agreed to provide a dataset that has been fully de-identified in accordance with HIPAA's safe harbor method — all 18 categories of identifiers have been removed, including names, dates (generalized to year only), geographic data below state level, and all other identifiers. The dataset contains aggregated statistical information about prescription patterns, ED visit frequencies, and demographic categories (age ranges, gender distributions).

The hospital's biostatistician, Dr. Marcus Webb, personally oversaw the de-identification process and has certified in writing that the dataset meets the safe harbor standard under §164.514(b)(2). The resulting dataset is labeled as "de-identified" in the hospital's data governance system.
narrative.question: Can Regional Medical Center share this fully de-identified statistical dataset with Professor Park for her opioid research study?

scenarios.title: Pharmaceutical Company Seeking Patient Records for Marketing

narrative.situation:
PharmaCorp International, a large pharmaceutical manufacturer, recently received FDA approval for Glucovex, a novel GLP-1 receptor agonist for Type 2 diabetes management. The company's marketing division has approached Memorial Hospital's administration with a business proposal: they would like the hospital to provide a list of patients currently diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes, along with their contact information and current medication regimens, so PharmaCorp can send targeted direct mail advertisements about Glucovex.

PharmaCorp's regional sales manager, Derek Foster, met with Memorial Hospital's Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Patricia Nguyen, and the hospital's marketing liaison, Beth Collins, to discuss the arrangement. PharmaCorp offered to pay Memorial Hospital $15 per patient record provided. No patient authorizations have been obtained or planned — PharmaCorp argues that since the information would "benefit patients by informing them of new treatment options," authorization shouldn't be necessary.

The hospital's privacy officer, Janet Morris, has been asked to review whether this arrangement is permissible. She's aware that marketing uses of PHI have special restrictions under HIPAA but wants to confirm the legal basis for her response.
narrative.question: Can Memorial Hospital share patient diagnosis records and contact information with PharmaCorp for a direct marketing campaign about their new diabetes drug, without obtaining patient authorizations?

expected_proof.explanation: Marketing disclosures of PHI require valid authorization under §164.508(a)(3). No authorization has been obtained. The face-to-face and nominal-value gift exceptions under §164.508(a)(3)(i) don't apply here (this is direct mail, not face-to-face). The payment arrangement ($15/record) constitutes sale of PHI, which is separately prohibited under §164.502(a)(5)(ii). No other pathway permits marketing disclosures without authorization.

scenarios.title: Anonymous Caller — Not By Name — DENY

narrative.situation: Someone calls Riverside Hospital's front desk asking about 'the woman who was in a car accident yesterday.' The caller does not identify themselves, doesn't provide the patient's name, and claims to be a 'family friend.' The patient, Angela Davis, did not object to the facility directory, but the directory system requires requests to be made by the patient's name. The caller cannot provide the name and instead describes physical characteristics and the accident details. The receptionist is unsure whether to provide any information.
narrative.question: Can the hospital share patient information with an anonymous caller who doesn't ask for the patient by name?

expected_proof.explanation: §164.510(a): facility-directory disclosure requires the requester to ask for the patient by name. An anonymous caller who cannot name the patient -- only describing physical characteristics and circumstances -- does not satisfy that condition, so the directory exception does not apply. No other pathway (authorization, TPO, 512 exception) applies either; denied under the closed-world assumption.

scenarios.title: Meridian Health Plan — Genetic Info Used for Underwriting

narrative.situation: Meridian Health Plan is reviewing Carla Nguyen's application file. During a prior wellness screening, Meridian obtained Carla's genetic test results (a BRCA gene panel) for an unrelated purpose. Meridian's underwriting team now wants to use those genetic test results internally to help set Carla's premium and coverage terms for a new individual policy.
narrative.question: May Meridian Health Plan use Carla Nguyen's genetic information for underwriting purposes?

expected_proof.blocking_fact: attribute = "genetic-info" AND purpose = "underwriting-and-related-purposes" AND sender is a health plan
expected_proof.explanation: §164.502(a)(5)(i): "Notwithstanding any other provision of this subpart," a health plan may not use or disclose genetic information for underwriting purposes -- an absolute prohibition that overrides any positive pathway. Without the genetic-info attribute (i.e. for an ordinary medical record), the identical fact set is otherwise permitted under §164.506(c)(1) as the covered entity's own TPO use -- confirmed by re-running with the attribute swapped to "medical-record", which flips the verdict to ALLOW.

scenarios.title: Access Health Insurance — Underwriting-Restricted PHI Reused for Quality Study

narrative.situation: Access Health Insurance evaluated Maria Lopez's application for an individual health policy last year and obtained her complete medical history as part of underwriting. Maria ultimately purchased coverage from a competing insurer instead. Access Health's internal quality-improvement team now wants to reuse Maria's medical file, still on hand from the underwriting review, for an unrelated healthcare-operations study on chronic disease trends. For the study, the quality-improvement team extracts only the specific diagnosis codes and chronic-condition indicators relevant to the disease-trends analysis from Maria's file, not her complete underwriting record.
narrative.question: May Access Health Insurance use Maria Lopez's medical records, originally collected for underwriting, for its quality-improvement study?

expected_proof.blocking_fact: received_phi_for_underwriting holds AND health_insurance_placed_with is absent AND the current purpose is not itself underwriting
expected_proof.explanation: §164.514(g): a health plan that received PHI for underwriting may not use it for other purposes when the individual did not end up placing insurance with that plan -- this is a cross-cutting negative norm that overrides any positive pathway (here, §164.506(c)(1), the CE's own healthcare-operations TPO use, would otherwise fire). Confirmed by re-running with health_insurance_placed_with("maria_lopez", "access_health_insurance") added, which flips the verdict to ALLOW.

narrative.situation: Sunrise Health System's compliance office is preparing a business-planning report for its board of directors. Rather than requesting the aggregated utilization statistics the report actually requires, the compliance office pulls complete, unredacted medical records for every patient in the system, including full psychiatric and substance-abuse treatment histories.
narrative.question: Is Sunrise Health System permitted to use patients' complete medical records for its business-planning report?

expected_proof.blocking_fact: no believes_minimum_necessary fact, and none of the six §164.502(b)(2) exceptions apply (not treatment, not to the individual, no authorization, not to the Secretary, not required by law, not a compliance requirement)
expected_proof.explanation: §164.502(b): minimum necessary is a constraint on top of any positive pathway, not a pathway of its own. §164.506(c)(1) (own TPO use, since business-planning is a healthcare-operations sub-purpose) fires, but minimum_necessary_satisfied fails because there is neither a belief-fact nor an applicable §164.502(b)(2) exclusion, so the top-level gate blocks it regardless. Confirmed by re-running with believes_minimum_necessary added, which flips the verdict to ALLOW.

scenarios.title: Lakeview Clinic — Unauthorized Sale of Diagnosis Records to a Data Broker

narrative.situation: MediData Analytics pays Lakeview Clinic a per-record licensing fee to obtain patients' diagnosis records, which MediData compiles into a database it resells to pharmaceutical marketing firms. Lakeview has not obtained written authorization from any of the affected patients, and the disclosure is not for treatment, payment, healthcare operations, research, or public health purposes. For each patient, Lakeview provides only the diagnosis code -- omitting other chart content such as visit notes, medications, and identifying details beyond what MediData's licensing contract specifies as the data fields covered.
narrative.question: May Lakeview Clinic disclose patients' diagnosis records to MediData Analytics in exchange for a per-record fee, without patient authorization?

expected_proof.blocking_fact: receives_remuneration_for_phi holds and none of the statutory sale-of-PHI exclusions (public health, research, TPO, business associate, individual access, required by law) apply
expected_proof.explanation: §164.508: remuneration in exchange for PHI, outside the eight statutory exclusions, is a "sale of PHI" requiring specific authorization (§502(a)(5)(ii)); none was obtained, so require_authorization_by_164_508 blocks every pathway. Confirmed by re-running with obtained_authorization_164_508 added for the same parties, attribute, and purpose, which flips the verdict to ALLOW.

scenarios.title: County General Hospital — Lab Tech Snooping on a Non-Patient's Chart

narrative.situation: Dana, a lab technician at County General Hospital, is not assigned to and has never treated a local news anchor who was admitted for surgery. Curious after seeing the anchor's name on a hallway census board, Dana repeatedly looks up the anchor's chart in the hospital's EHR system over several days and shares screenshots with friends, describing her access afterward as "checking on a patient." Each time, Dana views only the anchor's basic admission and status screen -- she does not open the anchor's full chart, lab results, or physician notes.
narrative.question: Is Dana's repeated access to the news anchor's medical record permitted under HIPAA?

expected_proof.blocking_fact: lacks_authorized_relationship holds -- Dana has no genuine treatment/operational need despite the nominal "treatment" purpose label
expected_proof.explanation: lacks_authorized_relationship is a cross-cutting negation guard in hipaa_top.dl that blocks the TPO pathway when a workforce member's access isn't backed by an actual care relationship, regardless of what purpose label the access is framed under (§164.506(c)(1)/(c)(2) would otherwise both fire on these facts, since self-dispatch by a provider role satisfies both the CE's-own-TPO and treatment-activities leaves). Confirmed by re-running with the lacks_authorized_relationship fact removed, which flips the verdict to ALLOW.

scenarios.title: Westside OB Clinic — Records Sent to the Wrong Address After a Confidential-Communication Request

narrative.situation: Jamie Doe, a patient at Westside OB Clinic and a survivor of domestic violence, formally requested that all communications and mailed records be sent only to a confidential P.O. box for her safety, and the clinic agreed. When Jamie later asks for a copy of her own records, Westside OB Clinic mails them to her home address on file instead of the P.O. box she specifically requested.
narrative.question: Is Westside OB Clinic permitted to send Jamie Doe's records to her home address after she requested confidential communication to a different address?

expected_proof.blocking_fact: sent_via_non_requested_channel holds -- the clinic granted a confidential-communication request but sent via a different channel anyway
expected_proof.explanation: §164.522(b): once a covered entity accommodates a reasonable request for confidential communications, sending PHI via a channel the individual did not request violates that accommodation -- a cross-cutting guard that overrides the otherwise-unconditional §164.502(a)(1)(i) individual-access pathway. Confirmed by re-running with the sent_via_non_requested_channel fact removed, which flips the verdict to ALLOW.
